big: This list has been burned by people selling them bought names, so anything that smells like a vendor is dead on arrival. The email gives something away, and the only ask is the states they lend in. That reply is easy to send, it qualifies them, and it means the promise is true when we keep it, because we pull the posts after they answer. We can't merge a live count into a bulk send, so the copy claims no count at all.

1A: This is the give-first offer, made true without a number. It says who we are, why these posts are no use to us, and that they can have them. There's no pitch and no call ask. The reply is one line: their states.
1B: It opens on the objection they already have. It says outright that we're not selling a list, then shows how the give works: they get the link and reply themselves. For readers who've been burned, that detail is the proof.
1C: This one names their real problem: the borrower with a solid deal who is short on gap or down payment. It puts the partnership on the table with no pay talk, and we still give first.
2A: The source used a real quote here, which a bulk send can't carry. So this describes the post plainly and invents nothing.
2B: 'What's the catch' is the question they're asking. This answers it in two sentences.
3A: The source's last touch. The offer stays open, with no pressure and nothing to buy.
3B: The person on the list often isn't the one who talks to new borrowers. This gives them an easy way to pass it on.

subsequences: These go only to people who replied. The list goes first. The ask for referrals comes in the last email, after we've already given something. The not-now email goes out about three months later, which matches the reply they got.
replies: The reply agent sends these as written, with no spintax. Funding replies go to your queue, so these are drafts for you until that changes. The word 'leads' stays out of every email to this list, by rule. Pay, terms or anyone upset goes to Justin.
